summary.text: A stationary distribution is a special distribution for a Markov chain: if the chain starts with it, the distribution over states stays the same at every later time.
If the chain is irreducible, the stationary distribution is always unique when it exists.
When the chain is irreducible and aperiodic, it can be read as the limiting distribution, and it relates to eigenvectors with eigenvalue one.

facts.label: Defining feature
facts.value: Starting in it keeps the state distribution the same at all times

facts.label: Uniqueness
facts.value: Unique if it exists, assuming irreducibility

facts.label: Limiting role
facts.value: The limiting distribution when the chain is irreducible and aperiodic

facts.label: Linear algebra link
facts.value: Related to eigenvectors with eigenvalue one

facts.label: Other name
facts.value: Called a stable distribution in some fields

paragraphs.heading: A distribution that stays put
paragraphs.text: A stationary distribution is a special way of spreading probability across the states of a Markov chain. Its defining feature is that it does not change over time. Suppose the chain starts out with its states weighted according to the stationary distribution. Then at any later time, the chance of finding the chain in each state is still given by exactly that same distribution. The idea applies both to Markov chains that move in discrete time steps and to those that run in continuous time.

paragraphs.heading: When there is only one
paragraphs.text: For an irreducible chain, there can be at most one stationary distribution: whenever one exists, it is unique. Whether one exists at all is a separate question. A sufficient sign is positive recurrence. If every state of an irreducible chain is positively recurrent, then a stationary distribution exists, and by the first point it is the only one.

paragraphs.heading: Where the chain settles
paragraphs.text: The stationary distribution also describes the long run. When a chain is both irreducible and aperiodic, the stationary distribution can be read as its limiting distribution. In other words, it is the distribution the chain tends toward over time, so it tells you how likely each state is after the chain has been running for a long while.

paragraphs.heading: Unchanged by a matrix
paragraphs.text: Seen more broadly, a stationary distribution is a particular object that some matrix or operator leaves exactly as it was. In this wider sense it need not be unique. That is why stationary distributions are tied to eigenvectors whose eigenvalue is one. Roughly speaking, many related ideas are all specific cases of this one general concept.

paragraphs.heading: A note on names
paragraphs.text: Some fields of application use the term stable distribution for what is here called a stationary, or marginal, distribution. In probability and statistics, however, stable distribution has a rather different meaning. So when the phrase turns up, it is worth checking which of the two meanings is intended.
